mainTopic: Who is exempt from קריאת שמע among the comforters in the row, and how far כבוד הבריות (human dignity) can override a מצוה, compared with חילול השם
overview: The גמרא first explains the משנה about comforters standing in a row (שורה). A ברייתא says that those who can see the mourners are exempt from קריאת שמע, while רבי יהודה says it depends on whether they came for the mourner's sake. This leads to a bigger question: when does כבוד הבריות (human dignity) override Torah law? רב rules that one who finds כלאים in his clothing must remove it even in the marketplace, because 'there is no wisdom against God,' and where there is חילול השם we do not even honor a teacher. The גמרא then tests this rule against several sources. A mourner's path through impurity and כהנים jumping over coffins to greet kings both turn out to involve only rabbinic impurity, which honor may set aside. The ברייתא saying that dignity overrides a Torah prohibition is explained by רב כהנא as referring to rabbinic laws, which rest on לא תסור. The lost-object exemption for a זקן comes from an explicit פסוק, and it cannot be extended because we do not learn איסורים from ממון. Finally, the גמרא begins a ברייתא about the extra word 'ולאחותו', which teaches that one must become impure for a מת מצוה, and the challenge from it continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Which row of comforters is exempt from קריאת שמע
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about those standing in the row and brings a ברייתא: a row that can see inside is exempt, and a row that cannot see inside is obligated.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'Those standing in the row, etc.' The רבנן taught: A row that sees inside is exempt, and one that does not see inside is obligated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה about comforters lined up in a row (שורה) and brings a ברייתא that explains which row is exempt from קריאת שמע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said that some people in the row are exempt and others are obligated. The ברייתא gives the test: if you can see the mourners' area ('inside'), you are actively comforting them and you are exempt. If you cannot see it, you are not really involved, so you must say שמע.

keyTerms.meaning: A row of comforters lined up to console the mourners after a burial
'The Rabbis taught.' This introduces a ברייתא.
That can see inside, toward the mourners

phrases.english: Those standing in the row, etc.
The Rabbis taught:
A row that sees inside is exempt,
and one that does not see inside is obligated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the discussion of the משנה's case of the row.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Comforters in a row that can see the mourners are exempt from שמע. Those who cannot see them are obligated.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: it depends on why you came
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says that those who came for the mourner's sake are exempt, and those who came for their own reasons are obligated.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: Those who come for the sake of the mourner are exempt. Those who come for their own sake are obligated.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה gives a different test for who in the row is exempt from שמע. For him, what matters is the person's reason for being there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion looked at physical position, meaning whether you can see inside. רבי יהודה looks at intention. Someone who came to honor and comfort the mourner is busy with a מצוה and is exempt. Someone who came out of curiosity is not, so he must say שמע.

keyTerms.meaning: Because of the mourner, meaning to honor and comfort him
Because of themselves, meaning for their own purposes, such as curiosity

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
Those who come on account of the mourner are exempt,
those who come on account of themselves are obligated.

steps.whatToRemember: The exemption from שמע in the row depends either on being able to see the mourners (first opinion) or on coming for the mourner's sake (רבי יהודה).
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different test from the first opinion in the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The exemption depends on intention. Coming for the mourner exempts you. Coming for yourself does not.

steps.title: Removing כלאים even in the marketplace
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that if someone finds כלאים in his clothing, he must take the garment off immediately, even in public.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: One who finds כלאים in his garment must take it off, even in the marketplace.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new, broader topic. It asks whether a person's dignity can push off a Torah prohibition, and it starts with רב's strong ruling about כלאים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taking off clothes in the street is very embarrassing. Still, רב says you may not wait until you get home, because you would keep wearing a Torah-forbidden mixture of wool and linen. Here human dignity does not override the prohibition.

keyTerms.meaning: A forbidden mixture. Here it means שעטנז, wool and linen in one garment.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
One who finds kilayim in his garment
must remove them even in the marketplace.

steps.whyThisMatters: This ruling becomes the test case for the whole sugya about כבוד הבריות against Torah prohibitions.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The comforters' exemption out of honor for the mourner leads the גמרא to ask more generally how far honor can go against מצוות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone wearing כלאים must remove the garment right away, even in public.

steps.title: The verse and the principle behind Rav's ruling
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives the source: 'There is no wisdom… against God.' From it comes the rule that wherever there is חילול השם, we do not even give honor to a teacher.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? 'There is no wisdom, no understanding, and no counsel against God.' Wherever there is חילול השם, we do not give honor even to a teacher.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for רב's reason and answers with a פסוק from משלי. It then turns that פסוק into a general rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק teaches that no human consideration can stand 'against God.' So when keeping a person's honor would mean violating God's command, which is a חילול השם, the honor gives way. This applies even to the honor owed to a רב, which is a very high level of respect.

keyTerms.meaning: We do not give honor to the teacher

phrases.english: What is the reason?
"There is neither wisdom, nor understanding,
nor counsel against the Lord" (משלי 21:30).
Anywhere that there is desecration of God's name
one does not show respect to the teacher.

steps.whatToRemember: The principle: where there is חילול השם, even a רב's honor does not count. Human dignity does not override an explicit Torah prohibition.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the scriptural basis and general principle behind רב's ruling.
steps.raayaObject: רב's ruling that כלאים must be removed even in public
steps.raayaSupportSource: משלי 21:30, 'אין חכמה ואין תבונה ואין עצה לנגד ה׳'

steps.title: A ברייתא: comforters follow the mourner even on an impure path
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: after a burial, if the mourner takes the impure path, everyone goes with him on the impure path out of respect for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged from a ברייתא: They buried the dead and were returning. In front of them were two paths, one pure and one impure. If he (the mourner) took the pure path, they went with him on the pure path. If he took the impure path, they went with him on the impure path, because of his honor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up a challenge to רב's principle by quoting a ברייתא. This step only lays out the case. The actual question comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The impure path passes graves, so walking on it makes a person טמא, which is especially a problem for כהנים. Even so, the ברייתא allows people to take that path to honor the mourner. This looks like honor overriding a prohibition, which is the opposite of רב's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: 'They objected.' This introduces a challenge from a תנאי source.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
They buried the dead and returned,
and before them were two paths,
one pure and one impure.
If he comes on the pure path, they come with him on the pure path;
if he comes on the impure path, they come with him on the impure path
because of his honor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source that seems to conflict with the principle in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The principle that honor does not override a prohibition when there is חילול השם
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא lets people become impure for the mourner's honor, so honor seems to override a prohibition.

steps.title: Why doesn't 'no wisdom against God' apply here?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: why may they walk on the impure path? The rule 'no wisdom against God' should apply here too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why? Let us say 'There is no wisdom and no understanding against God'!
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא states the challenge outright. Based on רב's principle, the ברייתא should not permit going on the impure path for the mourner's honor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse from step 4 says no human consideration stands against God. If so, the mourner's honor should not permit becoming טמא. The ברייתא and רב's principle seem to clash directly.

phrases.english: Why?
Let us say: "There is neither wisdom,
nor understanding… against the Lord!"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the contradiction set up by the ברייתא in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's permission to take the impure path, measured against רב's principle
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If no honor stands against God, the mourner's honor cannot permit טומאה.

steps.title: רבי אבא: the impure path is only rabbinically impure
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא explains that the ברייתא is talking about a בית הפרס, which is impure only by rabbinic law. Honor can override a rabbinic rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא explained it as referring to a בית הפרס, which is impure only by rabbinic law.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא answers the challenge. He says the 'impure path' in the ברייתא is a בית הפרס, whose impurity is only מדרבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בית הפרס is a field where a grave was plowed over, so the חכמים worried that bones were scattered and declared the field impure. Since this is only a rabbinic rule, the חכמים allowed it to give way to a mourner's honor. רב's principle still holds for Torah prohibitions like כלאים.

keyTerms.meaning: He explained it, meaning he interpreted the ברייתא
A field where a grave was plowed up. It is impure out of doubt about scattered bones.
By rabbinic law, not Torah law

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba explained it
as referring to a beit haperas, which is impure by rabbinic law.

steps.whatToRemember: כבוד הבריות can override a rabbinic prohibition (like בית הפרס) but not a Torah prohibition (like כלאים).
steps.confusionAlert: רבי אבא does not say the path is not impure at all. It is truly impure, but only מדרבנן, and that is why the mourner's honor can push it aside.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the key distinction in the sugya: human dignity can override rabbinic laws but not explicit Torah laws.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in steps 5 and 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the case: the ברייתא refers to rabbinic impurity only
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We assumed the impure path was impure by Torah law, so honor would be overriding a Torah prohibition.
steps.terutzMaskana: The path is a בית הפרס, impure only מדרבנן. Honor overrides a rabbinic prohibition, so רב's principle stands for Torah law.

steps.title: Proof that בית הפרס is only a rabbinic impurity
steps.stepSummary: Two lenient rulings, from שמואל and from רב, show that בית הפרס is only a rabbinic impurity.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: a person may blow on the dirt of a בית הפרס as he walks through it. And רב יהודה בר אשי said in the name of רב: a בית הפרס that people have walked over until it is trampled down is pure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves רבי אבא's claim from the last step: בית הפרס is only a rabbinic impurity. It brings two rulings that treat it very leniently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a real Torah impurity, we would never let someone simply blow the dirt away to look for bones. We would also never call an area pure just because people walked over it. Since the rules for בית הפרס are this relaxed, it must be a rabbinic stringency, which honor is allowed to override.

keyTerms.meaning: A field where a grave was plowed over, so bones may be scattered. Its impurity is rabbinic.
Blows (he blows the dust away to check for bones).
That has been trampled down (walked over until a path forms).

steps.whatToRemember: בית הפרס is only a rabbinic impurity. That is why the mourner and the people with him may take that path for the sake of honor.

phrases.english: As Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
A person may blow on (the dust of) a beit haperas and walk on.
phrases.notes: He blows the dust away to uncover any bones, steps around them, and keeps walking.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה בַּר אָשֵׁי מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב:
phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda bar Ashi said in the name of Rav:
A beit haperas that has been trampled down is pure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up רבי אבא's answer by proving that בית הפרס is rabbinic.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that בית הפרס is impure only by rabbinic law.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמואל (one may blow on the dust and walk) and רב (a trampled בית הפרס is pure).

steps.title: Priests jumped over coffins to greet kings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings רבי אלעזר בר צדוק's report that כהנים jumped over coffins to greet kings, even kings of other nations.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבי אלעזר בר צדוק said, 'We would jump over coffins of dead people to go greet the kings of Israel.' And they said this not only about the kings of Israel, but even about the kings of the nations, so that if a person merits it, he will be able to see the difference between the kings of Israel and the kings of the nations.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source that seems to show honor overriding Torah law. This step sets up the source; the actual question comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר בר צדוק was a כהן. A כהן may not become impure from the dead by Torah law, and passing over a coffin seems to make him impure. Even so, the כהנים did it just to honor kings, and the impurity here looks much more serious than a rabbinic בית הפרס.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear (introduces a source to prove or challenge something).

steps.confusionAlert: The reason given for greeting non-Jewish kings is not mainly about honoring them. It is so a person will see their glory and later understand how much greater the glory of the kings of Israel will be in the future redemption.

phrases.aramaic: תָּא שְׁמַע דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בַּר צָדוֹק:
phrases.english: Come and hear, as Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok said:

phrases.aramaic: מְדַלְּגִין הָיִינוּ עַל גַּבֵּי אֲרוֹנוֹת שֶׁל מֵתִים,
phrases.english: We would jump over coffins of the dead,
(to go) toward the kings of Israel.

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא לִקְרַאת מַלְכֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בִּלְבַד אָמְרוּ
phrases.english: And they did not say this only about (going) toward the kings of Israel,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אֲפִילּוּ לִקְרַאת מַלְכֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם,
phrases.english: but even toward the kings of the nations of the world,
so that if he merits (to see the redemption),

phrases.aramaic: יַבְחִין בֵּין מַלְכֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לְמַלְכֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם.
phrases.english: he will (be able to) tell the difference between the kings of Israel and the kings of the nations of the world.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בַּר צָדוֹק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new challenge against the rule of step 4, now involving what looks like a Torah-level impurity.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule from step 4 that honor never overrides where there is חילול השם.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Setup: כהנים seem to break the Torah ban on impurity from the dead just to honor kings.

steps.title: Why doesn't 'no wisdom against God' apply here?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the כהנים were allowed to do this, since 'no wisdom against God' should stop them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why? Let us say here too: 'There is no wisdom, no understanding, and no counsel against God'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks its question about the source it just brought. How could כהנים become impure just to honor a king?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is stronger than the earlier challenge. The answer of בית הפרס being rabbinic does not seem to work here, because impurity from a coffin sounds like real Torah-level impurity.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us say (we should apply this here).

phrases.english: Why?
Let us say: 'There is no wisdom and no understanding
and no counsel against God'!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמַּאי? לֵימָא אֵין חׇכְמָה וְאֵין תְּבוּנָה וְאֵין עֵצָה לְנֶגֶד ה׳
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the source from step 9 into a direct challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that honor gives way wherever there is חילול השם (step 4).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If even a teacher's honor gives way to God's law, then honor for a king surely should not allow a כהן to break a Torah ban on impurity.

steps.title: רבא's rule: a טפח of space blocks impurity
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers with רבא: by Torah law, a covering with a טפח of empty space blocks impurity, and one without that space does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is like רבא said. רבא said: By Torah law, a tent (covering over a dead body) that has a טפח of empty space blocks the impurity. One without a טפח of empty space does not block the impurity.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its answer by bringing a rule from רבא about when a covering blocks impurity. This rule sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If there is a טפח of air between the body and its cover, the impurity stays trapped inside, and nothing above becomes impure by Torah law. If there is no טפח of space, the impurity rises up through the cover. So jumping over a coffin is not automatically a Torah problem.

keyTerms.meaning: A tent or covering over impurity.
Blocks the impurity (stops it from spreading).

phrases.english: (It is) like Rava.
For Rava said: By Torah law, a tent,
any (tent) that has a handbreadth of empty space,
blocks the impurity.
And one that does not have a handbreadth of empty space
does not block the impurity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts answering the challenge of step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reclassifies the case: the impurity is rabbinic, not Torah-level.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Jumping over any coffin breaks the Torah ban on a כהן becoming impure.
steps.terutzMaskana: By Torah law, a coffin with a טפח of space blocks the impurity, so no Torah ban is broken.

steps.title: The coffin ban is only a decree, not applied for kings
steps.stepSummary: Most coffins have a טפח of space, so the ban on them is only rabbinic, and the רבנן did not apply their decree when honoring kings.
steps.simpleTranslation: Most coffins have a טפח of empty space. The רבנן made a decree about coffins that have the space because of coffins that do not. But for the honor of kings, the רבנן did not make this decree.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies רבא's rule to finish its answer. Jumping over most coffins breaks only a rabbinic decree, and honoring kings is allowed to set that aside.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By Torah law, a coffin with a טפח of space is not a problem. The רבנן still forbade it, because people might confuse it with a coffin that has no space. When they made this decree, they left out the case of honoring kings. So no Torah law was ever pushed aside, and the rule of 'no wisdom against God' stands.
steps.whatToRemember: Honor can push aside a rabbinic rule, like בית הפרס or the coffin decree, but so far it has not pushed aside a Torah law. Later the סוגיא finds a case where the Torah itself allows it (step 21). Both challenges were answered by showing that only a rabbinic rule was involved.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the general pattern of the סוגיא: כבוד הבריות can override rabbinic rules, but not Torah prohibitions.

phrases.aramaic: וְרוֹב אֲרוֹנוֹת יֵשׁ בָּהֶן חָלָל טֶפַח.
phrases.english: And most coffins have a handbreadth of empty space.
And they made a decree about those that have (the space)
because of those that do not have (it).
But because of the honor of kings,
the Sages did not make the decree in their case.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרוֹב אֲרוֹנוֹת יֵשׁ בָּהֶן חָלָל טֶפַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רבא's rule from step 11 to the coffins and finishes the answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows that only a rabbinic decree was involved, and the decree itself left out the honor of kings.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The כהנים broke a Torah law to honor kings.
steps.terutzMaskana: They broke only a rabbinic decree, and that decree was never made for the case of honoring kings.

steps.title: A ברייתא says human dignity overrides a Torah prohibition
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: כבוד הבריות is so great that it pushes aside a לא תעשה in the Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: Great is human dignity, because it pushes aside a negative commandment in the Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source that seems to clash with the rule 'no wisdom against God.' It is setting up the challenge that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the rule was that a Torah prohibition is never set aside for human honor. This ברייתא says plainly that כבוד הבריות does override a לא תעשה. That looks like a direct contradiction of the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear. This introduces a source brought as proof or as a challenge.
Human dignity, the honor owed to people
A negative commandment, a Torah prohibition

phrases.english: Come and hear:
Great is human dignity
for it overrides a prohibition in the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a new source in the ongoing test of the 'no wisdom against God' rule
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule אין חכמה ואין תבונה ואין עצה לנגד ה׳
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If human dignity overrides a Torah prohibition, then human considerations can stand against God's law.

steps.title: Why does dignity win against God's law?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how this can be, since the פסוק says no human wisdom can stand against God.
steps.simpleTranslation: But why? Let us say: 'There is no wisdom, no understanding, and no counsel against God'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states the challenge outright. How can the ברייתא let human dignity beat a Torah law?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק from משלי teaches that no human value outweighs God's command. The ברייתא seems to say the opposite. So something needs to be explained.

phrases.english: But why?
Let us say: 'There is no wisdom and no understanding
and no counsel against the Lord'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the contradiction raised by the ברייתא
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's claim that כבוד הבריות overrides a לא תעשה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A Torah prohibition should never yield to a human value, because of the פסוק.

steps.title: The prohibition meant is לא תסור
steps.stepSummary: רב בר שבא explains that the 'Torah prohibition' in the ברייתא is the לאו of לא תסור, the command to obey the חכמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב בר שבא explained it in front of רב כהנא as referring to the prohibition of 'you shall not turn aside.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב בר שבא answers that the ברייתא is talking about one specific לאו, which is לא תסור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: לא תסור is the Torah's command not to stray from what the חכמים teach. So the ברייתא really means that human dignity overrides rabbinic laws. It does not override ordinary Torah prohibitions.

keyTerms.meaning: He explained it, he interpreted it
The prohibition 'do not turn aside' from the words of the חכמים (דברים 17:11)

phrases.english: Rav bar Shaba interpreted it
before Rav Kahana
as referring to the prohibition of 'you shall not deviate.'

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּרְגְּמַהּ רַב בַּר שְׁבָא קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by narrowing which prohibition the ברייתא means
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא) to one specific prohibition
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא lets dignity override any Torah prohibition.
steps.terutzMaskana: It only overrides לא תסור, which means rabbinic laws.

steps.title: The students laugh: לא תסור is also Torah law
steps.stepSummary: The listeners laughed at רב בר שבא, because לא תסור is itself a Torah prohibition like any other.
steps.simpleTranslation: They laughed at him: Isn't the prohibition of 'you shall not turn aside' from the Torah?!
steps.whatsHappening: The students reject רב בר שבא's answer and laugh at it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their point is that לא תסור is written in the Torah too. So picking it out solves nothing. Why should dignity override this Torah לאו any more than another one?

phrases.english: They laughed at him:
the prohibition of 'you shall not deviate' is from the Torah!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer just given
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רב בר שבא's whole answer
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: לא תסור is a Torah לאו, so the original question comes right back.

steps.title: רב כהנא defends the answer
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא explains that all rabbinic laws lean on לא תסור, and the רבנן themselves allowed their own laws to give way for human dignity.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: A great man said something, do not laugh at him. All the words of the חכמים were attached to the prohibition of 'you shall not turn aside,' and because of human dignity the חכמים permitted it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא defends רב בר שבא and explains what he really meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every rabbinic law gets its Torah backing from לא תסור. That is why the ברייתא can call a rabbinic law a 'Torah prohibition.' But the חכמים who made these laws chose to let them give way to כבוד הבריות, so no actual Torah law is being overridden.

keyTerms.meaning: A great man, a significant scholar
They based them on, they attached them to

steps.whatToRemember: כבוד הבריות can override rabbinic laws only. They are called 'Torah prohibitions' because they rest on לא תסור. A real Torah prohibition does not give way to human dignity.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read the ברייתא as saying that dignity overrides real Torah laws like eating forbidden food. It only means rabbinic laws, which are tied to the Torah through לא תסור.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basis in הלכה for setting aside rabbinic prohibitions because of כבוד הבריות.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said:
A great man has said something,
do not laugh at him.
All matters of the Rabbis
were based on the prohibition of 'you shall not deviate,'
and because of human dignity the Rabbis permitted them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב כָּהֲנָא: גַּבְרָא רַבָּה אָמַר מִילְּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends step 15 against the rejection in step 16
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since לא תסור is a Torah לאו, dignity would be overriding Torah law.
steps.terutzMaskana: The רבנן built a built-in exception for dignity into their own laws, so the Torah itself is not overridden.

steps.title: New challenge from returning lost objects
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the פסוק 'והתעלמת מהם,' which teaches that sometimes you may ignore a lost object.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'And you shall ignore them' teaches that sometimes you ignore them and sometimes you do not ignore them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new challenge from the laws of returning a lost object. It is setting up a question that steps 19 and 20 complete.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra word 'והתעלמת' shows that in some cases a person is exempt from the Torah מצוה of returning a lost object. The coming discussion will ask whether this exemption is because of human dignity, which would mean dignity overrides a Torah law.

keyTerms.meaning: And you shall ignore them (דברים 22:1, about lost animals)

phrases.english: Come and hear: 'And you shall disregard them' —
at times you disregard them,
and at times you do not disregard them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After closing the ברייתא branch, the גמרא brings another source to test the rule
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule אין חכמה ואין תבונה ואין עצה לנגד ה׳
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If sometimes one may ignore a lost object, perhaps human dignity is setting aside a Torah מצוה. Steps 19 and 20 develop the full challenge.

steps.title: The three cases where one may ignore a lost object
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא lists three cases where a person may ignore a lost object: a כהן when the object is in a cemetery, a זקן for whom it is beneath his dignity, and someone whose own work is worth more than his friend's loss.
steps.simpleTranslation: How so? If he was a כהן and the object is in a cemetery, or he was an elder and it is beneath his dignity, or his own work was worth more than his friend's, for this the Torah says 'and you shall ignore'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting the ברייתא from the last step. It explains when the Torah lets you ignore a lost object.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The middle case matters most for our סוגיא. A זקן may ignore a lost object only because handling it is undignified. So here human dignity pushes aside the Torah מצוה of returning lost objects, and that is what the גמרא will challenge in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: How so? (introduces an explanation of cases)
A priest, who may not become impure from the dead
And you shall ignore (the Torah's word that allows ignoring)

steps.confusionAlert: The case of the כהן has nothing to do with dignity. He may not enter the cemetery at all. Only the case of the זקן is about כבוד הבריות.

phrases.english: How so?

phrases.aramaic: אִם הָיָה כֹּהֵן, וְהִיא בְּבֵית הַקְּבָרוֹת,
phrases.english: If he was a priest, and it (the object) is in the cemetery,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ הָיָה זָקֵן וְאֵינָהּ לְפִי כְבוֹדוֹ,
phrases.english: or he was an elder and it is not fitting for his dignity,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ שֶׁהָיְתָה מְלַאכְתּוֹ מְרוּבָּה מִשֶּׁל חֲבֵרוֹ,
phrases.english: or his own work was worth more than his friend's (loss),
for this it is said: 'and you shall ignore'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא introduced in step 18 by listing its cases.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that כבוד הבריות cannot override a Torah prohibition
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The case of the זקן shows dignity overriding the Torah מצוה of returning lost objects.

steps.title: Why doesn't 'no wisdom against God' apply here?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the זקן may ignore the object. We should say 'there is no wisdom and no counsel against God' here too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why? Let us say: 'There is no wisdom, no understanding, and no counsel against God'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes the challenge clear. If dignity can never override a Torah law, how can the זקן ignore the lost object?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 4 the פסוק 'אין חכמה' was used to show that human dignity cannot override a Torah law. Here the גמרא points to a Torah law that does give way to dignity. The two ideas seem to contradict each other.

phrases.english: Why?
Let us say: 'There is no wisdom and no understanding
and no counsel against God'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: States the actual challenge drawn from the ברייתא in step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: The principle from step 4 that dignity cannot override a Torah prohibition
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא shows a Torah obligation giving way to the dignity of a זקן.

steps.title: The Torah itself wrote the exception
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the lost object case is different, because the Torah itself wrote 'והתעלמת מהם'.
steps.simpleTranslation: There it is different, because it is written: 'and you shall ignore them'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. In the case of lost objects, the Torah itself made the exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Human reasoning is not overriding the Torah here. The Torah wrote the allowance into the מצוה itself, so 'אין חכמה לנגד ה׳' does not apply.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean dignity in general overrides Torah law. It only shows that in this one מצוה the Torah itself allowed it.

phrases.english: There it is different,
because it is written: 'and you shall ignore them'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Special verse (גזירת הכתוב) limited to this case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The זקן's exemption shows that dignity generally overrides Torah law.
steps.terutzMaskana: The exemption comes from an explicit פסוק, so it is not human wisdom against God.

steps.title: Can we learn a general rule from the lost object case?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: since we found one Torah law that gives way to dignity, why not learn from it that dignity overrides all prohibitions?
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us learn from it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests using the lost object case as a model for all Torah laws. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the Torah allowed dignity to override one מצוה, maybe that shows a general principle. Then dignity would override other prohibitions too.

phrases.english: And let us learn from it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 21 by trying to expand it into a general rule.
steps.kashyaTarget: Limiting the answer in step 21 to lost objects only
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A פסוק in one area might be a model (בנין אב) for all Torah prohibitions.

steps.title: We don't learn prohibitions from money laws
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. We do not learn laws about איסורים from laws about ממון.
steps.simpleTranslation: We do not learn a prohibition from a money law.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא blocks the attempt to make the lost object case a general rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Returning a lost object is about money, and money laws are more easily flexible. Real prohibitions are stricter, so a leniency in a money law cannot be carried over to them.
steps.whatToRemember: The lost object case shows dignity overriding a Torah law only because the Torah wrote it there. Since it is a money law, it cannot teach a general rule about איסורים.
steps.whyThisMatters: 'איסורא ממונא לא ילפינן' is a general rule of derivation that appears throughout ש״ס.

phrases.english: A prohibition from a money law
we do not learn.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion of step 22.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects generalizing from lost objects to all prohibitions
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A money law cannot serve as a source for ritual prohibitions.

steps.title: A new source: the נזיר and his sister
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא. It asks what the word 'ולאחותו' in the passage about the נזיר comes to teach. It answers that if a man was on his way to slaughter his קרבן פסח or to give his son a ברית מילה and heard that a relative died, he should not go back and make himself impure.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: Why does the Torah say 'and for his sister'? Suppose a man was going to slaughter his פסח and circumcise his son, and he heard that a relative died. I might think he should go back and become impure. You said: he shall not become impure.
steps.whatsHappening: With 'תא שמע' the גמרא brings another source to challenge רב's principle. It begins quoting a ברייתא about the extra word 'ולאחותו', setting up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Slaughtering the פסח and ברית מילה are serious מצוות with the punishment of כרת. The ברייתא teaches that even the honor of a dead relative does not push them aside. This prepares the next part of the ברייתא, about a מת מצוה.

keyTerms.meaning: What does the verse come to teach?

steps.confusionAlert: This part is not yet the proof. It only sets up the ברייתא, and the point about dignity comes in its next line, which is next.

phrases.english: Come and hear.
'And for his sister', what does it come to teach?

phrases.aramaic: הֲרֵי שֶׁהָיָה הוֹלֵךְ לִשְׁחוֹט אֶת פִּסְחוֹ,
phrases.english: Suppose one was going to slaughter his Paschal lamb,
and to circumcise his son,
and he heard that a relative of his died,
I might think he should go back and become impure?
You said: he shall not become impure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the lost object proof was limited, the גמרא opens a new proof from נזיר.
steps.raayaObject: Whether כבוד הבריות can override a Torah prohibition
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's principle (step 4) that human dignity does not override a Torah prohibition
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Setup: the ברייתא will conclude that one who may not become impure must still become impure for a מת מצוה, so the dignity of the dead seems to override a Torah prohibition.

steps.title: The extra word 'his sister' limits the ban to relatives, not an unattended corpse
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא raises a possible thought: just as a person going to do the פסח or מילה cannot become impure for his relatives, maybe he also cannot become impure for a מת מצוה. It answers from the word 'ולאחותו': only for his sister may he not become impure. This prepares the conclusion that he must become impure for a מת מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have thought: just as he does not become impure for his relatives, so too he does not become impure for a מת מצוה. That is why the verse says 'and for his sister.' It is only for his sister that he does not become impure.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא raises a mistaken idea and uses the word 'ולאחותו' to start correcting it. It is setting up its next line, which comes at the start of the next amud and says he does become impure for a מת מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 24, the ברייתא said a person going to bring a קרבן פסח or do a ברית מילה may not become impure even for a close relative. Now it asks whether that ban also covers a מת מצוה, and limits it with the word 'his sister.' The point is that his sister has others to bury her, but a מת מצוה has no one. That is why the ban stops there.

keyTerms.meaning: 'I might have thought.' This word opens a mistaken idea that the ברייתא is about to correct.
Makes himself impure, here through contact with a dead body.
An unattended dead body that has no one else to bury it. Burying it is a duty that falls on whoever finds it.
'The verse teaches.' This phrase brings the verse that settles the question.
'And for his sister.' This word in the verse about the נזיר is read as a limit on the ban.

steps.confusionAlert: This line does not say a sister is less important than a stranger. The difference is that his sister has other people to bury her, while a מת מצוה has nobody. The issue is the dignity of the dead person, not closeness of family.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the heart of the גמרא's challenge. If a person who is forbidden to become impure must still become impure for a מת מצוה, then the dignity of the dead (כבוד הבריות) seems to override a Torah prohibition, against רב's principle.

phrases.english: I might have thought: just as he does not become impure for them (his relatives)
phrases.notes: 'Them' refers to the close relatives mentioned in the ברייתא in step 24.

phrases.english: so too he does not become impure for a מת מצוה (an unattended corpse)
phrases.notes: This is the mistaken idea that the ברייתא is about to reject.

phrases.english: the verse teaches: 'and for his sister'
phrases.notes: The verse comes from the laws of the נזיר (במדבר ו:ז).

phrases.english: it is for his sister that he does not become impure,
phrases.notes: The ban applies only to cases like his sister. The ברייתא's next line, at the start of the next amud, adds that he does become impure for a מת מצוה.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָכוֹל: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁאֵינוֹ מִטַּמֵּא לָהֶם כָּךְ אֵינוֹ מִטַּמֵּא לְמֵת מִצְוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues quoting the ברייתא brought as proof in step 24, moving from the ban on relatives to the limit on that ban.
steps.raayaObject: That כבוד הבריות can override a Torah prohibition. Here that means the burial of a מת מצוה overriding the ban on becoming impure.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's reading of the extra word 'ולאחותו' in the laws of the נזיר.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's principle (step 4) that human dignity does not override a Torah prohibition
